My dad passed away from liver cancer a little under a year ago. Two years before that, I stopped visiting and talking to my family in California while I was living in New Jersey. I felt helpless watching everyone dismiss conversations about mental and physical health, no matter how gently or urgently I tried to bring them up.

Over time, I realized that a family’s culture is built from the accumulation of everyday habits, beliefs, coping mechanisms, and choices. Some people naturally carry more influence than others- especially fathers in patriarchal Asian families like mine- but I also believe families can slowly change when individuals begin taking agency over their own lives.

Coming home to care for my dad during the last month of his life changed me deeply. I could suddenly see more clearly how years of stress, silence, avoidance, resentment, unhealthy habits, and emotional burdens shaped all of us- including me. I realized my own silence and anger were also part of the story.

One of the hardest things in some families is learning how to speak honestly without feeling like you’re betraying your parents or disrespecting tradition. In my family, questioning our parents’ choices almost felt forbidden. But I’ve learned that staying silent can quietly damage your own heart too.

What you’re doing is incredibly brave. I think healing often begins with one person being willing to change themselves first- to speak honestly, live differently, and interrupt the cycle with love instead of autopilot. It’s messy and painful sometimes, but those small shifts slowly begin changing the family culture itself.

Thank you for sharing your story. It resonated with me deeply. ❤
